rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Friction opposes attempted or actual relative motion along surfaces. **Static friction self-adjusts** up to the limiting value μ_sN; kinetic friction runs at μ_kN, slightly smaller and nearly speed-independent. rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - f_max = μN; f_k = μ_k N - Angle of repose: μ = tan θ_r - Incline: N = mg cos θ; a = g(sin θ − μ cos θ) - Pull up at constant speed: F = mg(sin θ + μ cos θ)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Static vs. Kinetic Threshold:** The maximum static friction $f_s^{\max} = \mu_s N$ is the *upper bound* for static friction. Static friction is a *variable* force that matches the applied force up to this limit. Kinetic friction $f_k = \mu_k N$ applies *only* when sliding occurs, with $\mu_k < \mu_s$.  ·  **Normal Force Dependency:** Friction is proportional to the *normal reaction*, not the weight. Any vertical force component (pulling up, pushing down, incline) changes $N$, which directly changes the friction force. Always compute $N$ first.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Static friction is NOT always μ_sN — it is a variable force that matches the applied force up to that maximum.  ·  The normal force is NOT always mg — on a slope it is mg cos θ; with pulling/pushing at an angle it changes.

rows.text: ***5 kg block, μ_s = 0.4*** — needs just over 20 N to start (NEB 2023).

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **Numerical (3m): A 20 kg block is pulled up a 30° incline (μ = 0.25) at constant speed. Find the required force (g = 10).** — F = mg(sin θ + μ cos θ) = 200(0.5 + 0.25×0.866) = 200 × 0.7165 = 143.3 N.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **Friction is self-adjusting:** static friction matches your push exactly until the limiting value — then motion begins.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Laws: opposes relative motion; f ∝ N; independent of contact area; kinetic friction independent of speed; μ_k < μ_s.  ·  Angle of repose: μ = tan θ_r.  ·  Incline: N = mg cos θ; sliding a = g(sin θ − μ cos θ); pull up at constant speed F = mg(sin θ + μ cos θ).

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Anti-lock brakes keep tyres rolling rather than sliding because kinetic friction is smaller than peak static friction — maximum stopping force comes just below sliding.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — The Force That Opposes Every Push Friction is the contact force opposing relative (or attempted) motion between surfaces. It is indispensable — walking, brakes, nail grips — and costly — worn engines, wasted fuel. The syllabus asks for the laws of solid friction and their experimental verifications, plus incline numericals.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts | Term | Definition | |---|---| | **Static friction** | Opposes the *start* of motion; self-adjusting up to a maximum | | **Limiting friction** | Maximum static friction just before sliding begins: $f_s^{max} = \mu_s N$ | | **Kinetic friction** | Opposes motion once sliding: $f_k = \mu_k N$, roughly constant and slightly less than limiting friction |…  ·  ## 3. Worked Numericals **Q1 (3m, 2023):** A block of mass 5 kg rests on a horizontal plane. The coefficient of static friction is 0.4. What horizontal force is needed to start the block moving? (g = 10 m/s²) $N = mg = 50$ N; $f_{limiting} = \mu_s N = 0.4 \times 50 = 20$ N.…

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Area Independence (Ideal Model):** The laws of friction assume friction is independent of the apparent contact area (Coulomb's model). This holds well for dry, rigid surfaces but breaks down for soft materials, lubricated contacts, or adhesive forces where real contact area matters.  ·  **Static vs kinetic friction:** static self-adjusts up to μ_s N (starting is harder); kinetic is roughly constant at μ_k N and slightly smaller.  ·  **Friction vs normal reaction:** friction is proportional to N — press harder and it grows; lighten the load and it shrinks.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Friction can act in the direction of motion — static friction pushes you forward when walking.  ·  The angle of repose depends only on μ_s, not on the mass of the body.  ·  NEB frequently asks: 'Does the body slide? If so, find the acceleration' — check tan θ vs μ_s first.
